keyPoints: Modules are split into domain, data, presentation and app
Dependencies point one way: presentation and data depend on domain, and domain has no Android dependency
Brand customization lives in app-level DI wiring, not in if-branches inside business logic
A UI tweak for one brand leaks into shared business logic
A quick fix in the data layer ends up being depended on by a ViewModel
Changing one brand's behavior then requires regression-testing all brands
The compiler enforces the boundary, so a brand-specific bug cannot silently break another brand
It costs more upfront ceremony: interfaces and DI bindings
It pays off as soon as there are two or more cities or service variants

topic: the ticketing app with several transport services
keyPoints: One app bundled bike rental, car parking and public transport, and some cities also added boat rental
Each city had its own branding on top of the per-service differences
One interface per capability, with a separate implementation per service type and per city

topic: what to share in Kotlin Multiplatform
keyPoints: Share code when the business rule is identical across platforms and an abstraction costs less than two implementations
Do not share where a platform difference is load-bearing
UI-adjacent logic is cheaper to write twice
Backend communication end to end: request handling, response parsing and mapping into domain models
A platform just calls a shared function and gets back a ready-to-use model
No parsing or mapping logic was duplicated per platform

topic: what stayed platform-specific in Kotlin Multiplatform
keyPoints: All UI (Compose and SwiftUI)
Local storage and the database
Anything touching the system: permissions, platform APIs, background work scheduling
expect/actual declarations are a real maintenance surface
A shared interface with a platform-specific implementation can drift out of sync between iOS and Android
Mitigated by tests written once against the shared logic and run on both platform targets

topic: AI in PR security review against OWASP MASVS
keyPoints: MASVS defines verification requirements across categories, and manual checking of every PR does not scale
A checklist-per-category approach was handed to Copilot to run during PR review
The output is a risk assessment of candidate findings, not an automatic approve or block gate

topic: findings from the MASVS security audit
keyPoints: One audit pass surfaced 10 real findings across the applicable MASVS categories
Critical: JWT access, refresh and ID tokens stored in plaintext SharedPreferences
High: the ID token is never invalidated on logout

topic: why AI security findings need a human reviewer
keyPoints: Findings are candidates for a human to confirm, not ground truth
False positives that block merges erode trust, and false negatives on security are unacceptable
Every merge or apply decision went through a human, and fixes were a separate follow-up task

topic: false positives in the security scan
keyPoints: Three false positives were flagged, all with the same root cause: a hardcoded-credential pattern matching token-like literals
The literals were in test fixtures and mocks, for example a tok_123 payment token in a JUnit test
Mitigated by excluding test source sets from the scanned scope

topic: why the domain module has no Android dependency
keyPoints: domain is plain Kotlin (kotlin.jvm) with no Android Gradle plugin
Business rules can be unit-tested on the plain JVM
It stays portable if the Kotlin Multiplatform goal happens
